title: वैदिक शिक्षण विधि : श्रवण, मनन, निदिध्यासनः र वर्तमान शिक्षण प्रणालीमा उपादेयता
nepali: आधुनिक पश्चिमी शिक्षा प्रणालीले वैदिक दर्शनमा निहित शैक्षिक विचारहरूमा छायाँ पारिरहेको परिवेशमा वैदिक ग्रन्थमा के कस्ता शिक्षण विधिहरू छन् भन्ने जिज्ञासा समाधान गर्ने ध्येयले यो लेख तयार गरिएको छ । उपनिषद्मा वर्णित तत्वज्ञानका विधिलाई कसरी बुझ्न सकिएला ? ती विधिहरूको वर्तमान शिक्षा व्यवस्थामा के उपादेयता हुन सक्ला ? भन्ने दुई प्रश्नहरूको उत्तर खोज्न यो लेख केन्द्रित छ । शास्त्रहरूको अध्ययन गरी त्यसमा निहित अर्थको व्याख्या गर्न प्रचलित हर्मेन्यूटिक विधिको प्रयोगद्वारा सूचना निर्माण र व्याख्या गरिएको छ । उपनिषदमा वर्णित श्रवणलाई विभिन्न छ चरणमा अर्थपूर्ण तरिकाले सुन्ने प्रक्रियाको रूपमा बुझ्न सकिँदो रहेछ । श्रवण गरिएको ज्ञानलाई वाद, जल्प र वितण्डा जस्ता प्रक्रियाहरूबाट स्वीकार, इन्कार वा मूल्याङ्कन गर्ने प्रक्रिया मनन रहेछ । मननबाट सुनिश्चित वा सन्देहरहित भएकोज्ञानलाई व्यवहारमा रूपान्तरण गर्ने प्रक्रियालाई निदिध्यासन भनिँदो रहेछ । यी विधिहरू विशेष रहेछन् । तत्वज्ञानका अभिलाषी साधकहरू र सांसारिक ज्ञानआर्जन गर्न चाहने विद्यार्थीहरू दुवैका लागि यी विधिहरू फलदायी रहेछन् । अनौपचारिक र औपचारिक शिक्षाका तल्ला तहदेखि उच्च तहसम्मका जुनसुकै विषयको शिक्षणमा पनि यी विधिहरू सान्दर्भिक देखिन्छन् । यसले वैदिक ग्रन्थहरूको उपादेयता पुष्टि गर्छ । वैदिक चिन्तन परम्परामा यस्ता उपयोगी ज्ञानहरू धेरै हुन सक्छन, जुन हामीलाई थाहा नभई रहेको हुन सक्छ । अतः प्राज्ञिक समुदायले वैदिकग्रन्थहरूको अध्ययन अनुसन्धानमा चासो राख्नुपर्ने देखिन्छ ।
american_english: This article has been prepared with the aim of resolving the curiosity about what kinds of teaching methods exist in the Vedic texts, in a setting in which the modern Western education system is casting a shadow over the educational ideas embedded in Vedic philosophy. How might the method of tattvajnana described in the Upanishads be understood? What usefulness could those methods have in the present education system? This article is focused on seeking answers to these two questions. Information has been generated and interpreted through the use of the hermeneutic method current for interpreting the meaning contained in the scriptures after studying them. The shravana described in the Upanishads turns out to be understandable as a process of listening meaningfully in six different stages. Manana turns out to be the process of accepting, rejecting or evaluating heard knowledge through processes such as vada, jalpa and vitanda. The process of transforming knowledge that has become certain or doubt-free through manana into practice is called nididhyasana. These methods are special. These methods turn out to be fruitful for both aspirants longing for tattvajnana and students who wish to gain worldly knowledge. These methods look relevant in the teaching of any subject at any level, from the lower to the higher levels of informal and formal education. This confirms the usefulness of the Vedic texts. There may be many such useful pieces of knowledge in the Vedic tradition of thought, which may be there without our knowing it. Therefore, the academic community appears to need to take an interest in the study and research of the Vedic texts.
british_english: The present article has been prepared with the object of settling the enquiry as to what manner of teaching methods are to be found in the Vedic texts, in a climate in which the modern Western system of education is casting a shadow over the educational ideas enshrined in Vedic philosophy. How is one to understand the method of tattvajnana set out in the Upanishads? Of what value might those methods prove to be in the present system of education? The present article is directed towards seeking answers to these two questions. Information has been constructed and interpreted by employing the hermeneutic method in current use for expounding the meaning contained in the scriptures, having first studied them. The shravana described in the Upanishads proves to be understandable as a process of listening in a meaningful manner at six different stages. Manana proves to be the process of accepting, rejecting or appraising knowledge that has been heard, by means of procedures such as vada, jalpa and vitanda. The process of converting knowledge rendered certain, or free from doubt, by manana into practice is termed nididhyasana. These methods are singular. These methods prove profitable both to aspirants desirous of tattvajnana and to students wishing to acquire worldly knowledge. These methods appear pertinent to the teaching of any subject whatsoever, from the lower to the higher levels of informal and formal education. This vindicates the usefulness of the Vedic texts. In the Vedic tradition of thought there may well be many such useful bodies of knowledge, which may be there without our being aware of them. It therefore appears that the scholarly community ought to take an interest in the study and research of the Vedic texts.
australian_english: This article has been put together with the aim of answering the question of what sort of teaching methods are found in the Vedic texts, at a time when the modern Western education system is throwing a shadow across the educational ideas sitting inside Vedic philosophy. How are we meant to make sense of the tattvajnana method set out in the Upanishads? What real worth could those methods have in the education system we have now? This article sets out to find answers to these two questions. The information has been built up and interpreted by way of the hermeneutic method that is standard for unpacking the meaning held in the scriptures, after studying them. Shravana, as the Upanishads describe it, comes across as a process of listening in a meaningful way across six stages. Manana comes across as the process of accepting, knocking back or weighing up knowledge that has been heard, through processes like vada, jalpa and vitanda. Turning knowledge that manana has made certain, or free of doubt, into practice is what gets called nididhyasana. These methods are something out of the ordinary. These methods come across as worthwhile for both aspirants chasing tattvajnana and students keen to pick up worldly knowledge. These methods look relevant to teaching any subject at all, right from the lower levels through to the higher levels of informal and formal education. This backs up the worth of the Vedic texts. There could be plenty of useful knowledge of this kind in the Vedic tradition of thought, knowledge we might be carrying on with without ever knowing about it. So it looks like the academic mob needs to take an interest in studying and researching the Vedic texts.
informal_english: This piece was put together to settle the question of what sort of teaching methods you'd find in the Vedic texts, at a time when the modern Western education system is throwing its shadow over the educational ideas tucked away in Vedic philosophy. How would you ever get your head around the tattvajnana method the Upanishads talk about? And what use at all would those methods be in the education system we have now? That's the pair of questions this article goes after. I built up and read the information using the hermeneutic method that's going these days for working out the meaning inside the scriptures, once you've studied them. Shravana, the way the Upanishads tell it, turns out to be a matter of listening in a meaningful way across six stages. Manana turns out to be how you accept, turn down or weigh up what you've heard, through things like vada, jalpa and vitanda. And turning knowledge that manana has made certain, with no doubt left in it, into practice — sure that's what they call nididhyasana. These methods are a bit special, all the same. They work well for the aspirants who're mad for tattvajnana and for students who just want to get worldly knowledge — for the both of them. They look relevant for teaching any subject at all, from the bottom rungs to the top of informal and formal education. Which all goes to prove the worth of the Vedic texts. There could be plenty more useful knowledge like that in the Vedic way of thinking, sitting there unknown to us entirely. So the academic crowd would want to take an interest in studying and researching the Vedic texts, I'd say.
translator_notes: Single-paragraph abstract; the two research questions are kept as separate sentences with their governing sentence following, as in the source. Sanskrit technical terms (shravana, manana, nididhyasana, vada, jalpa, vitanda, tattvajnana) kept in transliteration as the source treats them as terms rather than glosses.
